claim: A navigation agent trained only on the standard continuous-navigation datasets carries over to a different navigation task and dataset, and to a physical robot in a workspace it has never seen, without any real-world fine-tuning. Supported only if it exceeds the strongest earlier system under the same transfer conditions on both success rate and path-weighted success, and succeeds in more than half of physical-robot trials, counting a trial successful only when the robot stops within one metre of the instructed target.

experiments: Build the agent and its supervision. Setup: start from an 8B vision-language model and train one epoch at learning rate 1e-5 using only the expert trajectories of the two standard continuous-navigation datasets. At every expert step, supervise a single sequence containing the progress label, the predicted outcome for each candidate action, the decision whether to write the observation into memory, its role label, and the ground-truth next action; all the non-action labels are generated by deterministic rules over the trajectory with a five-step lookahead, with no extra environment rollouts or manual annotation. Memory is a fixed queue of length 8. About 1,000 GPU-hours on eight A100s.

Does it transfer to a different navigation dataset and task? Setup: evaluate on the unseen split of an object-goal navigation benchmark. Result: 38.0 success and 26.9 path-weighted, against 35.2 / 19.6 and 37.1 / 19.8 for the two published comparators, so it leads on both measures, with the larger margin on path efficiency.

Does it transfer to a physical robot? Setup: deploy the simulation-trained agent unchanged on a wheeled robot with a front-facing camera and a 24 GB GPU, in a workspace it has not seen. Ten instructions involving visually similar objects and behaviours such as entering and leaving rooms, each repeated three times, counting success when the robot stops within one metre of the target. Result: 21 of 30 trials, a 70% success rate.
